gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Fitbit Charge 6's 'up to 7 days' drops to 3 days once the always-on display is turned on, and to 5 hours with its built-in GPS running. On that like-for-like basis, the $99.99 Amazfit Active 2 (21 h continuous GPS) and Garmin vívoactive 6 (21 h GPS-only) last about four times longer per GPS workout than the 'long-battery' tracker.
standout_why: I compared four rival pages. The cited Google Store Charge 6 spec page would not render, so I could not check it directly (see unsourced). The cited Apple Support 125093 page gives the 24 h and 38 h figures and the test footnote, but no workout or GPS hours. sekin.in gives the Charge 6's 7 days plus Apple's 24 h test conditions, and only says 'always-on display and SpO2 use more power' without a runtime or a GPS figure. itechguides.com (fitbit-vs-apple-watch-which-wearable-fits-your-needs) has no always-on, GPS or test-condition figures. None of them puts the bands and watches on the same basis: always-on display days and continuous-GPS hours. nymag.com could not be fetched.
decides: This confirms the pick by buyer type and corrects ChatGPT's '7 days vs 24 hours' framing. For a sleep and steps buyer, the band's battery lead holds but shrinks to 3 days with always-on display. For a runner or hiker, the band is the short-battery option: the Charge 6 lasts 5 h with GPS, against 21 h for the Active 2 ($99.99) and vívoactive 6 ($299.99 SRP). So 'running/sports' buyers should be pointed to a GPS-first watch, not a band. Apple's 24 h is a mixed-use day that already includes a 60-min workout and 6 h of sleep, so it is not comparable with Fitbit's unqualified 'up to 7 days'.
